title: Global growth shocks scar investment announcements unevenly, making geopolitical position part of economic recovery
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11452, The Scars of Global Growth Shocks: Evidence of Uneven Recovery in FDI Announcements
geography: Global cross-country and cross-sector foreign-direct-investment project-announcement data, with heterogeneity by country safety, strategic sector, institutions, and geopolitical alignment

observations.period: Global growth shocks; dynamic response of FDI project announcements

denominator.unit: global FDI project-announcement response estimated with local projections

scarring_duration.value: adverse global growth shocks have scarring effects on FDI project announcements for about three years

decision_timing.value: the analysis accounts for the real-time nature of investor decisions

mechanism.value: a temporary global downturn can become a persistent investment pipeline deficit rather than only a contemporaneous output movement

boundary.value: an announcement is an investment-intention measure and does not by itself establish project completion, capital expenditure, jobs, or household benefit

observations.method: Local-projection estimates using global growth shocks and FDI project-announcement outcomes, with dynamic horizons and robustness exercises.
observations.uncertainty: The estimated horizon and magnitude depend on shock definitions, announcement data, model specification, exposure, and the distinction between announced and realized projects; the paper does not establish a universal three-year effect for every shock.
observations.subgroup: Countries and sectors with different institutional conditions, geopolitical alignment, perceived safety, global exposure, and strategic importance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower announcements may reflect firms postponing or rerouting projects rather than permanently losing investment; announcements can also contain strategic signaling and may not map cleanly to realized activity.

observations.period: Global growth shocks; country safety and sectoral strategicness

safe_countries.value: scarring effects are more subdued in countries perceived as safer

strategic_sectors.value: projects in strategic sectors smooth headline announcement fluctuations because they are less sensitive to adverse global growth shocks

interpretation.value: security, strategic demand, and institutional credibility can buffer the investment pipeline when aggregate growth conditions deteriorate

distributional_route.value: investment buffering may protect some places and sectors while concentrating opportunity and bargaining power in already strategic or safer locations

observations.method: State-dependent and sectoral heterogeneity estimates using alternative definitions of safety, strategic sectors, and institutional conditions.
observations.uncertainty: Safety and strategicness are analytical classifications rather than direct measures of every investor's risk judgment, and buffered announcements do not prove equal local employment, supplier participation, or public benefit.
observations.subgroup: Advanced economies, emerging and developing economies, strategic and non-strategic sectors, firms with different cross-border exposure, and local labor markets.
observations.counterinterpretation: Strategic projects may be supported by state policy or geopolitical priorities and could generate weaker spillovers than ordinary private investment; safer-country effects may partly reflect stronger institutions or data coverage.

observations.period: Global growth shocks; geopolitical positioning and uneven recovery

geopolitical_position.value: geopolitical positioning plays an important role in the uneven recovery of FDI announcements

robustness.value: the result is robust across alternative shock measures, specifications, institutional definitions, sector definitions, and geopolitical-alignment measures

political_economy.value: economic recovery is partly conditioned by how a country is situated in a fragmented investment and security order, not only by domestic growth prospects

open_consequence.value: the allocation of future investment can reshape infrastructure dependence, employment options, local bargaining power, and public attribution of geopolitical alignment

observations.method: Robustness and heterogeneity exercises varying geopolitical-alignment definitions and institutional, sectoral, and shock measures.
observations.uncertainty: The paper identifies uneven announcement responses, not a complete causal account of alliance choice, investment completion, technology transfer, local political reaction, or household welfare.
observations.subgroup: Countries positioned differently in global political and economic networks, strategic industries, local workers, firms, governments, and communities receiving or losing investment prospects.
observations.counterinterpretation: Geopolitical alignment may proxy for security, market access, institutions, sanctions exposure, or expected policy stability; the observed relationship should not be read as a single alignment mechanism.

related_sources.claim: Official World Bank record for WPS11452, authors, metadata, topics, and reproducibility-package link.
Bibliographic record and abstract summarizing the three-year scarring horizon, safe-country, strategic-sector, geopolitical-positioning, and robustness results.
World Bank reproducibility package for the FDI-announcement scarring study.

boundary: This record adds geopolitical positioning and investment-pipeline scarring as a firm, state-power, and household-opportunity mechanism. It is not evidence that announced projects are completed, that FDI creates local jobs or welfare, or that geopolitical alignment alone causes the observed uneven recovery.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank PDF, document page, abstract record, and reproducibility metadata were reviewed for the dynamic FDI-announcement result, three-year scarring horizon, safe-country and strategic-sector heterogeneity, geopolitical-positioning result, robustness claims, and announcement-versus-realization boundary.
